documents.title: Management of Asymptomatic Bacteriuria in Adult Female Populations (AUGS Clinical Consensus Statement)
documents.doc_type: AUGS Clinical Consensus Statement (modified Delphi; 25 statements)
documents.citation: Siddiqui NY, Ackerman AL, Advani SD, et al. "Management of Asymptomatic Bacteriuria in Adult Female Populations." *Urogynecology (Phila).* 2025;31(9):827–845. doi:[10.1097/SPV.0000000000001731](https://doi.org/10.1097/SPV.0000000000001731)

key_points.point: Treat ASB only in pregnancy and before urologic procedures that breach mucosa; otherwise observe.
key_points.verbatim_quote: Treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB) is thought to confer more benefit than harm in 2 groups: pregnant women and patients undergoing urologic procedures with a break in a mucosal or tissue barrier. Outside of these 2 groups, antibiotic treatment does not reduce the rate of upper urinary tract infection or mortality, and observation is reasonable.

key_points.point: Harms of treating ASB, including in women with recurrent UTI (secondary analysis of 550 women: more resistant bacteria and more recurrences).
key_points.verbatim_quote: Treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB) is associated with worse clinical outcomes including longer length of hospital stay, increased readmission, and antibiotic associated adverse events including resistance, intolerances, allergic reactions, and C difficile infections.
key_points.location: Table 3, Q5 statement (evidence summary cites Cai 2015 secondary analysis of 550 women with rUTI)

key_points.point: Microbiological cure is not a treatment goal.
key_points.verbatim_quote: microbiological cure (eg, negative posttreatment urine culture) is not a goal in clinical practice.

key_points.point: Neurogenic bladder: antibiotic prophylaxis for ASB at urodynamics; otherwise do not treat ASB.
key_points.verbatim_quote: Individuals with ASB and neurogenic bladder dysfunction who are having urodynamic testing should receive prophylactic antibiotics.

key_points.point: Diabetes: do not treat ASB.
key_points.verbatim_quote: There are no data to support treatment of ASB in women with diabetes. Persistent or recurrent ASB is common in women with diabetes. Overall, the risk of progression to pyelonephritis or urosepsis is low.

key_points.point: Diabetes: ASB prevalence rises with HbA1c and SGLT2-inhibitor use.
key_points.verbatim_quote: Prevalence rises with increasing age and hemoglobin A1c values and in those using sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitor medications.

key_points.point: Renal transplant: CCS says treat ASB within the first 2 months (diverges from IDSA 2019 and EAU 2026).
key_points.verbatim_quote: ASB should be treated with antibiotics within the first 2 months of receiving a renal transplant to prevent transplant pyelonephritis, bacteremia, and rejection of the renal graft.

key_points.point: Prolapse: ASB not treated regardless of PVR; postoperative-catheter prophylaxis does not reduce UTI; day-of-surgery bacteriuria before urogynecologic surgery is linked to postoperative UTI (29.6% vs 5.6%, OR 7.2); selective screening for women with a history of rUTI was cost-effective.
key_points.verbatim_quote: Regardless of the postvoid residual (PVR), there is no evidence to suggest that women with prolapse and ASB should be treated except in situations when they develop symptoms of UTI.
key_points.location: Table 4, Q10 statement and summary of evidence (citing Fok 2013 J Urol; Hendrickson 2022 AJOG; Dieter 2014 Obstet Gynecol)

key_points.point: Women with baseline LUTS: an acute change should prompt urinalysis and culture, with no rescreening if symptoms do not improve.
key_points.verbatim_quote: For women with baseline LUTS, a change in LUTS symptoms should be evaluated with urinalysis and urine culture. If pyuria and bacteriuria are noted concurrent with the change in LUTS symptoms, then antibiotic therapy may be indicated. If LUTS symptoms do not improve with antibiotic treatment, there is insufficient evidence to support rescreening for bacteriuria.
key_points.location: Table 5 (Managing the Continuum Between ASB and UTI), Q14 statement

key_points.point: Delirium or mental status change with bacteriuria alone: look for other causes and observe rather than treat.
key_points.verbatim_quote: In women with bacteriuria who present with acute mental status changes (eg, delirium) but without local genitourinary symptoms or other systemic signs of infection (eg, fever or hemodynamic instability), consider assessment for other causes and careful observation rather than antimicrobial treatment.
key_points.location: Table 5, Q15 statement (see also Q13 for women who cannot report symptoms)

key_points.point: Intravesical instillations: no role in asymptomatic bacteriuria; may reduce symptomatic UTI in neurologically intact women with rUTI.
key_points.verbatim_quote: There is no evidence to support the practice of intravesical instillations to decrease bacteriuria or minimize progression to symptomatic UTI in those who are otherwise asymptomatic. In neurologically intact women suffering from recurrent urinary tract infections, bladder instillations may decrease the number of symptomatic UTIs, but there is no consensus on a standard formulation.

key_points.point: Nonantibiotic prevention for rUTI with intervening ASB; D-mannose is included, although the literature search predates MERIT.
key_points.verbatim_quote: For those with a history of recurrent UTI who also have intervening periods of ASB, we suggest that nonantibiotic options (eg, vaginal estrogen, methenamine hippurate, D-mannose, cranberry) can be utilized as agents to prevent symptomatic UTI while avoiding long-term antibiotics.

key_points.point: Persistent bacteriuria after treatment: avoid antibiotic courses aimed at urinary sterilization.
key_points.verbatim_quote: Repeated courses of antibiotics with the goal of urinary sterilization should be avoided. If symptoms have resolved after a full course of antibiotics, further treatment is not warranted.

key_points.point: Every woman with ASB or rUTI should have a pelvic examination and a PVR.
key_points.verbatim_quote: All women experiencing either ASB or recurrent UTI should undergo a pelvic examination with evaluation for possible prolapse and urinary postvoid residual determinations since these factors may assist clinicians in the recognition of confounding conditions that would benefit from alternative treatment.
key_points.location: Table 5, Q19 statement (evidence: 'assessment of PVR should be considered in all women presenting with recurrent UTI')

key_points.point: Extended culture and molecular or NGS testing: insufficient evidence and a risk of overtreatment.
key_points.verbatim_quote: For now, there is insufficient evidence that extended cultures or molecular testing for UTI provides improved management of women with urinary symptoms and these tests have the potential risk for overtreatment of bacteriuria.

key_points.point: Urinalysis is valuable for its negative predictive value.
key_points.verbatim_quote: When used as part of a diagnostic workup, urinalysis parameters should be leveraged for their negative predictive value instead of sensitivity or positive predictive value.

key_points.point: Threshold of ≥10³ CFU/mL for symptomatic women (superscript flattened to '≥103' in the extracted HTML).
key_points.verbatim_quote: Data support using thresholds of ≥10³ CFU/mL of a single uropathogen for confirming significant bacteriuria in symptomatic women.

key_points.point: Use a straight-catheter specimen when contamination is suspected or anatomy limits a clean catch, including significant POP.
key_points.verbatim_quote: When there is suspicion for vaginal or skin contamination in a urine sample (eg, squamous epithelial cells or mucus) or when anatomic factors limit the potential for obtaining a clean catch specimen (eg, wheelchair bound, significant pelvic organ prolapse, morbid obesity), straight catheterization should be performed to obtain a urine specimen.

key_points.point: Evidence currency: the literature search ran through 2022, so it predates MERIT (2024) and the 2025 AUA amendment.
key_points.verbatim_quote: The search was completed on October 14, 2021, and updated on January 2, 2023, by the information specialist. Results were limited to literature published between 1970 and 2022.

pages.section: Part XI: Management algorithm / Part V: Role of imaging and cystoscopy
pages.current_text_quote: **Flowmetry and postvoid residual (PVR)** — useful when impaired emptying is suspected.

Document symptoms together with pyuria and uropathogenic bacteria; an isolated positive culture or one historical culture does not explain every subsequent episode. Interpret colony count in the clinical and collection context, and repeat a contaminated specimen.
Do not obtain routine test-of-cure cultures in an asymptomatic patient; repeat cultures for persisting symptoms.

**Straight catheterization:** useful when repeated voided specimens are contaminated or reliable collection is not possible. Balance improved specimen quality against instrumentation discomfort and risk.

| **Symptomatic women with pyuria** | Lower counts, including ≥10² CFU/mL of a single plausible uropathogen in selected patients, can be clinically meaningful; account for contamination and laboratory reporting limits |

pages.section: Expanded Quantitative Urine Culture (EQUC) and Emerging Technologies
pages.current_text_quote: Molecular and sequencing methods can also detect colonizing organisms; a positive result is not, by itself, an indication for antibiotics.

pages.section: Asymptomatic Bacteriuria: When to Screen and Treat
pages.current_text_quote: Routine treatment is not recommended for older adults, diabetes, SCI, chronic urinary catheters, elective nonurologic surgery, or nonrenal solid-organ transplant recipients without a separate indication. Some settings remain evidence gaps, including the first month after renal transplantation and high-risk neutropenia
**Midurethral sling:** a 661-patient retrospective study did not find significantly fewer postoperative UTIs with preoperative culture screening in asymptomatic women.
Do not perform surveillance cultures or treat ASB solely because a woman has a history of rUTI.

pages.section: Asymptomatic Bacteriuria — When NOT to Treat
pages.current_text_quote: kidney transplantation is not a blanket indication to eradicate ASB. Evidence in the first month after transplant is insufficient; later routine treatment is not recommended

pages.section: Genitourinary Syndrome of Menopause (GSM) (no bacteriuria/delirium content anywhere on page)
pages.current_text_quote: **Vaginal estrogen reduces recurrent UTIs** — a major source of morbidity, hospitalization, and antibiotic use in elderly women.
**D-mannose is no longer routinely recommended.** The MERIT primary-care RCT is the largest, most rigorous, and negative.
It is an off-label, specialist option for selected refractory cases, particularly patients already catheterizing; routine instillation into every long-term catheter is not established.

**EAU recommends no antibiotic prophylaxis for UDS**; the **SUFU 2017 policy** instead recommends prophylaxis for defined risk groups, including NLUTD, elevated PVR, immunosuppression, age >70, asymptomatic bacteriuria, or catheter/device use.

**Asymptomatic bacteriuria is common, not universal.** Do not routinely screen or treat asymptomatic NLUTD patients; pregnancy and selected urologic procedures are exceptions requiring their specific guidance.
**Treat the reversible** — UTI, constipation, diuretic dosing, sleep apnea.
**Post-void residual (PVR)**: Obtain for voiding symptoms, recurrent UTI or concern about incomplete emptying

proposed_edits.section: Part XI: Management algorithm (step 1 vs step 6) and Part V flowmetry/PVR paragraph
proposed_edits.change: Move pelvic examination with prolapse assessment and PVR into step 1, the initial evaluation, instead of 'Further evaluation (if refractory)'. Keep flowmetry selective. Text: 'AUGS (2025 CCS, Q19) advises a pelvic examination with prolapse assessment and a PVR for every woman with rUTI or ASB. AUA 2025 (Statement 1 commentary) says emptying assessment can be considered for all patients and should be performed when incomplete emptying is suspected: significant anterior-wall prolapse, neurologic disease, diabetes or a sensation of incomplete emptying.' The current algorithm lists PVR only when refractory, which contradicts Q19.
proposed_edits.citation: Siddiqui NY, Ackerman AL, Advani SD, et al. Urogynecology (Phila). 2025;31(9):827–845. doi:10.1097/SPV.0000000000001731; plus existing ref3 (AUA/CUA/SUFU 2025)

proposed_edits.change: Add a short 'Baseline LUTS, OAB and bacteriuria' paragraph. (1) A change from baseline LUTS warrants urinalysis and culture; antibiotics may be indicated when pyuria and bacteriuria accompany the change. If symptoms do not improve, do not rescreen or retreat; consider mimics such as myofascial pain and IC/BPS (Q14). (2) Treating ASB in women with rUTI increased resistant strains and recurrences in the 550-woman secondary analysis (Q5; Cai 2015 CID). (3) Avoid antibiotic courses aimed at urinary sterilization. After two culture-directed courses without resolution, look for another cause or source (Q18). Do not import the evidence-summary suggestion to treat ≥10² CFU/mL with pyuria in refractory OAB as a recommendation; it rests on two small studies.
proposed_edits.citation: Siddiqui NY, et al. Urogynecology (Phila). 2025;31(9):827–845. doi:10.1097/SPV.0000000000001731; Cai T, et al. Clin Infect Dis. 2015;61(11):1655–1661. doi:10.1093/cid/civ696

proposed_edits.section: New subsection after 'Genitourinary Syndrome of Menopause (GSM)': 'Bacteriuria in Older Women'
proposed_edits.change: Add three points. (1) ASB rises with age: 10–50% of women over 65, higher in institutional settings (Q2). (2) Bacteriuria with acute mental status change but no local GU symptoms or systemic signs: look for other causes and observe rather than treat. With fever and no localizing source, assess and treat urinary and nonurinary sources empirically (Q15; Q13 for women who cannot report symptoms). (3) Treating ASB in delirious older inpatients was associated with poorer functional recovery (Dasgupta 2017, as summarized in the CCS). Frame this for the postoperative older urogyn or reconstructive patient.
proposed_edits.citation: Siddiqui NY, et al. Urogynecology (Phila). 2025;31(9):827–845. doi:10.1097/SPV.0000000000001731; IDSA 2019 (Nicolle LE, et al. Clin Infect Dis. 2019;68(10):e83–e110. doi:10.1093/cid/ciy1121)

proposed_edits.change: Extend the straight-catheterization bullet: obtain a catheterized specimen when contamination is suspected or anatomy limits a clean catch, e.g. significant pelvic organ prolapse, wheelchair use or morbid obesity. Note that squamous cells alone do not predict contamination, which is consistent with the existing bullet.

proposed_edits.change: In the 'Symptomatic women with pyuria' row, add that AUGS (2025) supports ≥10³ CFU/mL of a single uropathogen to confirm significant bacteriuria in symptomatic women, with ≥10² possible in selected patients. In the ASB row, note that AUA/CUA/SUFU treats bacteriuria of any magnitude without symptoms as ASB, versus the IDSA ≥10⁵ definition.
proposed_edits.citation: Siddiqui NY, et al. Urogynecology (Phila). 2025;31(9):827–845 (Q1, Q23). doi:10.1097/SPV.0000000000001731

proposed_edits.section: Expanded Quantitative Urine Culture (EQUC) and Emerging Technologies
proposed_edits.change: Add the urogynecology-society position. AUGS (2025 CCS, Q20) finds insufficient evidence that EQUC or molecular testing improves management, and warns of overtreatment. It sees no role for these tests in telling UTI from ASB and advises against treating fastidious organisms found only on molecular testing without compatible symptoms. Q21: no clinically available biomarker (e.g. IL-6) yet improves diagnosis.
proposed_edits.citation: Siddiqui NY, et al. Urogynecology (Phila). 2025;31(9):827–845. doi:10.1097/SPV.0000000000001731

proposed_edits.change: Add a urogynecologic-surgery bullet. Day-of-surgery bacteriuria (9.5% of 284 women) was associated with postoperative UTI despite standard prophylaxis (29.6% vs 5.6%; OR 7.2), with no pyelonephritis or urosepsis. Selective screening of women with a history of rUTI was cost-effective, and universal screening was not. Oral prophylaxis during postoperative catheterization did not reduce UTI. Verify and cite the primary papers directly, not only the CCS summary.

proposed_edits.change: Keep the current IDSA-based renal-transplant wording; do not adopt AUGS Q9. Optionally add one sentence noting the divergence: the AUGS 2025 CCS favours treating ASB within 2 months of renal transplant, while EAU 2026 (Strong) advises not to screen for or treat ASB in renal transplant recipients, citing RCTs that include the first 2 months. documents.notes: Full text read: the ASB CCS is free on LWW. I retrieved the article HTML with curl after WebFetch returned HTTP 402, then read all 25 statements (Tables 2–6) and the Discussion. The extracted HTML flattened superscripts ('≥105' means ≥10⁵; '≥103' means ≥10³); quotes restore the superscripts. Usefulness is high: it is the most urogyn-specific ASB document available and touches about 8 WARWIKI pages. Most pages already agree with it because they follow IDSA 2019 and AUA 2025. It adds three practice-relevant points: (a) pelvic exam and PVR for all women with rUTI or ASB (Q19), where the rUTI algorithm now defers PVR to refractory cases, a partial conflict graded P2 because AUA 2025 says emptying evaluation 'can be considered for all patients, but should be performed' when incomplete emptying is suspected; (b) managing bacteriuria against a background of baseline LUTS (Q14); (c) delirium or mental status change with bacteriuria (Q13/Q15), which is missing from the geriatric page. Two points where WARWIKI should NOT follow the CCS. First, Q9 on renal transplant: the CCS says treat within 2 months and claims IDSA agrees, but EAU 2026 strongly recommends against screening or treating ASB in renal transplant recipients, and WARWIKI's IDSA-based wording is defensible. Second, Q17 lists D-mannose, but the literature search stopped at 2022, before MERIT. Also do not promote the Q14 evidence-summary claim that ≥10² CFU/mL with pyuria in refractory OAB may justify antibiotics; it rests on two small studies. The CCS's own reference 1 lists IDSA 2019 with page numbers 1611–1615 and doi ciz021 rather than e83–e110 and ciy1121; cite IDSA from its original record. Delphi panel of 8 (7 urogyn/FPMRS and 1 ID).

documents.doc_type: AUGS Clinical Consensus Statement (systematic review + Delphi; 9 statements)
documents.citation: Dueñas-Garcia OF, Chung DE, Geynisman-Tan J, et al. "Diabetes Mellitus and Recurrent Urinary Tract Infections." *Urogynecology (Phila).* 2026;32(5):477–485. doi:[10.1097/SPV.0000000000001823](https://doi.org/10.1097/SPV.0000000000001823)

key_points.point: Women with diabetes have more UTIs and more recurrent UTIs; prospective and randomized evidence is lacking.
key_points.verbatim_quote: UTI and recurrent UTI prevalence are higher in women with diabetes mellitus, but there is a significant lack of prospective studies, including randomized trials, on the risks and side effects of medications related to lower UTIs in this population.

key_points.point: Nine statements across epidemiology, risk factors (glycemic control, glucose-lowering drugs, bacteriuria) and prevention/treatment. The statement text was not accessible.
key_points.verbatim_quote: Nine statements were developed and categorized into 3 areas: (1) epidemiology, (2) risk factors (glycemic control, glucose-lowering medications, and bacteriuria), and (3) prevention and treatment.

key_points.point: Evidence was too thin for a guideline, so the panel produced a consensus statement instead (32 studies, 1995 to Oct 2024).
key_points.verbatim_quote: Initially aiming to create clinical guidelines, insufficient evidence led to the development of a Clinical Consensus Statement, which was revised using the Delphi method.

key_points.point: Diabetes-specific prevention and treatment trials are urgently needed.
key_points.verbatim_quote: Future studies assessing the efficacy of UTI prevention and treatment strategies specifically in women with diabetes mellitus are urgently needed.

pages.section: Part III: Risk factors / Part IX: Special populations
pages.current_text_quote: | **Postmenopausal** | Vaginal atrophy / hypoestrogenism, urinary incontinence, cystocele, elevated postvoid residual, prior UTI history |

**Hold 3 days before elective surgery** (4 days for ertugliflozin), consistent with ADA (3–4 days), AHA/ACC 2024 (Class I) and US labeling for empagliflozin (at least 3 days) and ertugliflozin (at least 4 days).

proposed_edits.section: Part III: Risk factors (new 'Diabetes mellitus' row) and Part IX: Special populations (short 'Women with diabetes' entry)
proposed_edits.change: Add diabetes as a risk context. (1) UTI and rUTI prevalence are higher in women with diabetes, and diabetes-specific trial evidence is lacking (Dueñas-Garcia 2026). (2) ASB is common in diabetic women, rises with HbA1c and SGLT2-inhibitor use, and should not be treated (Siddiqui 2025, Q8). (3) AUA 2025 lists diabetes among reasons to assess for incomplete emptying. Cite only the abstract-level conclusion of the diabetes CCS until its nine statements (glycemic control, glucose-lowering medications including SGLT2 inhibitors, prevention/treatment) have been read in full text. Do not attribute specific SGLT2 or glycemic-target recommendations to it until then.
proposed_edits.citation: Dueñas-Garcia OF, et al. Urogynecology (Phila). 2026;32(5):477–485. doi:10.1097/SPV.0000000000001823; Siddiqui NY, et al. Urogynecology (Phila). 2025;31(9):827–845. doi:10.1097/SPV.0000000000001731; existing ref3 (AUA/CUA/SUFU 2025)

documents.notes: Access is abstract-only. LWW returned 402 to WebFetch, and curl returned only the abstract and 'In Brief' (not marked Free). There is no PMC or Europe PMC full text (subscription), and web searches found no copy of the statements. I did not read any of the nine statements and do not report them. Supporting points in the proposed edit come from documents I did read: the ASB CCS Q8 statement and evidence (SGLT2 and HbA1c association with ASB) and the local AUA 2025 unabridged Statement 1 commentary, which names diabetes as a reason to evaluate incomplete emptying. WARWIKI's rUTI page does not mention diabetes anywhere, and the risk-factor table omits it, so this is a real gap. The perioperative diabetes page covers SGLT2 holds for surgery, not UTI risk, so it is listed as unrelated with no edit; another session is currently editing that file. Medium usefulness: relevant to the urogyn rUTI population, but the actionable content cannot be verified without full text. Recommend a follow-up full-text read (institutional access) before quoting any statement.

pages.current_text_quote: The 2025 AUA / CUA / SUFU update emphasizes symptom-linked diagnosis, antimicrobial stewardship and informed choices among preventive options.

The 2025 AUA/CUA/SUFU guideline recommends urinalysis and culture/susceptibility testing for symptomatic episodes before treatment, with clinical judgment for selected self-start management while awaiting results.

documents.notes: Access is title-only. The LWW fulltext page (HTTP 402 to WebFetch, 200 to curl) shows only title, authors and citation, with no abstract or body. PubMed (PMID 41925625) has no abstract, and Ovid shows the same header. I did not read the commentary's reasoning and report none. What I could verify independently: the journal page for the 2018 statement (doi 10.1097/SPV.0000000000000550) is now titled '[WITHDRAWN]' and carries an indicator, 'An updated version of the article is available.', linking to the AUA recurrent-UTI guideline page. The PubMed record for the 2018 statement (PMID 29369839, last revised 2019) does not yet show a withdrawal link. A repo-wide grep of docs/ and src/ for the 2018 DOI, PMID or title found no WARWIKI page citing it. The rUTI and urine-studies pages already rest on AUA/CUA/SUFU 2025, so no P1 retired-statement citation exists and no edit is needed. Ref23 on the rUTI page (Smith AL et al. J Urol 2018 rapid review) is a different document, not the AUGS statement. Low usefulness: the notice only confirms current practice. Keep it in mind for future edits: do not cite Brubaker 2018 FPMRS as current AUGS guidance.

items.reason: Quotes are current. Line 98 (Part V) reads 'Flowmetry and postvoid residual (PVR) — useful when impaired emptying is suspected'. Lines 227-228 (step 6) read 'Further evaluation (if refractory): Flowmetry and PVR measurement.' Step 1 (line 217) mentions neither pelvic examination nor PVR. The At a glance bullet (line 15) already says 'review ... pelvic examination ... and possible incomplete emptying', so the page contradicts itself. I read the CCS full text (Ovid/LWW HTML via doi). Q19 statement: 'All women experiencing either ASB or recurrent UTI should undergo a pelvic examination with evaluation for possible prolapse and urinary postvoid residual determinations...' Its evidence summary is softer: 'assessment of PVR should be considered in all women presenting with recurrent UTI.' Q19 had the weakest Delphi agreement: 62.5% strongly, 37.5% weakly agree. The local AUA 2025 unabridged text makes Statement 1 (pelvic examination) a Clinical Principle, and its commentary says emptying evaluation 'can be considered for all patients, but should be performed in any patient with suspicion of incomplete emptying, such as those with significant anterior vaginal wall prolapse, underlying neurologic disease, diabetes, or a subjective sensation of incomplete emptying.' key_points.point: The guideline does not rank hormonal therapies or support a required stepwise sequence; decisions are made by shared decision-making.
key_points.verbatim_quote: Given that there is insufficient information to recommend one hormonal therapy over another, this guideline is not meant to support a stepwise progression through different hormonal approaches.

key_points.point: Local low-dose vaginal estrogen for GSM vulvovaginal symptoms is a Strong Recommendation, but the evidence grade is C.
key_points.verbatim_quote: Clinicians should offer the option of local low-dose vaginal estrogen to patients with GSM to improve vulvovaginal discomfort/irritation, dryness, and/or dyspareunia. (Strong Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C)
key_points.location: Statement 8, Hormonal Interventions (AUA unabridged guideline, local file aua-sufu-augs-gsm-2025.txt)

key_points.point: Patients on systemic estrogen can still be offered local estrogen or vaginal DHEA.
key_points.verbatim_quote: In patients with GSM who are on systemic estrogen therapy, clinicians should offer the option of local low-dose vaginal estrogen or vaginal dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA). (Expert Opinion)

key_points.point: Vaginal estrogen may be offered as an adjunct when GSM coexists with OAB.
key_points.verbatim_quote: In patients with GSM and comorbid genitourinary conditions (e.g., overactive bladder), clinicians may offer the option of local low-dose vaginal estrogen to improve genitourinary symptoms. (Expert Opinion)

key_points.point: For GSM with recurrent UTI, vaginal estrogen is recommended (Moderate, Grade B).
key_points.verbatim_quote: In patients with GSM and recurrent urinary tract infections, clinicians should recommend local low-dose vaginal estrogen to reduce the risk for future urinary tract infections. (Moderate Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade B)

key_points.point: Moisturizers and lubricants are a graded recommendation and can be used alone or with other therapies.
key_points.verbatim_quote: Clinicians should recommend the use of vaginal moisturizers and/or lubricants, either alone or in combination with other therapies, to improve vaginal dryness and/or dyspareunia in patients with GSM. (Moderate Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C)

key_points.point: Supplements are not supported, and patients should avoid irritants.
key_points.verbatim_quote: Clinicians should counsel patients that the evidence does not support the use of alternative supplements in the treatment of GSM. (Expert Opinion)

key_points.point: The evidence does not support energy-based devices for GSM outcomes.
key_points.verbatim_quote: Clinicians should counsel patients that the evidence does not support the use of CO 2 laser, ER:YAG laser, or radiofrequency in the treatment of GSM-related vulvovaginal dryness, vulvovaginal discomfort/irritation, dysuria, quality of life, change in bothersome symptoms, satisfaction with treatment, or dyspareunia. (Moderate Recommendation, Evidence Level: Grade C)

key_points.point: There is a narrow expert-opinion exception for CO2 laser, which must be disclosed as experimental outside trials.
key_points.verbatim_quote: In the context of shared decision-making, and with the disclosure that these therapies are considered experimental outside of clinical trials, clinicians may consider CO 2 laser treatment in patients who are not candidates for, or prefer alternatives to, FDA-approved treatments for GSM-related vulvovaginal dryness, vulvovaginal discomfort/irritation, dysuria, and/or dyspareunia. (Expert Opinion)

key_points.point: Breast cancer counseling (statement 19): tell patients there is no evidence linking local estrogen to breast cancer.
key_points.verbatim_quote: Clinicians should inform patients of the absence of evidence linking local low-dose vaginal estrogen to the development of breast cancer. (Expert Opinion)

key_points.point: Breast cancer survivors: local estrogen may be recommended with multidisciplinary shared decision-making. The statement does not require prior failure of nonhormonal therapy.
key_points.verbatim_quote: For patients with GSM who have a personal history of breast cancer, clinicians may recommend local low-dose vaginal estrogen in the context of multi-disciplinary shared decision-making. (Expert Opinion)

key_points.point: Counsel that vaginal DHEA and ospemifene do not increase breast cancer risk (expert opinion), even though their labels carry warnings.
key_points.verbatim_quote: Clinicians should counsel patients with GSM that neither vaginal dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) nor ospemifene increase the risk for breast cancer. (Expert Opinion)

key_points.point: Endometrial counseling for local estrogen is a Moderate Recommendation. The evidence covers 8–36 weeks of use.
key_points.verbatim_quote: Clinicians should counsel patients with GSM that local low-dose vaginal estrogen, does not increase the risk for endometrial hyperplasia with atypia or endometrial cancer. (Moderate Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C)
key_points.location: Statement 22 (discussion: 'neither endometrial cancer nor hyperplasia was found after 8 to 36 weeks')

key_points.point: The same endometrial counseling applies to DHEA and ospemifene.
key_points.verbatim_quote: Clinicians should counsel patients with GSM that neither vaginal dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) nor ospemifene increase the risk for endometrial hyperplasia with atypia or endometrial cancer. (Moderate Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C)

key_points.point: No endometrial surveillance solely because of these agents.
key_points.verbatim_quote: Clinicians should not perform endometrial surveillance in patients with GSM solely due to their use of local low-dose vaginal estrogen, vaginal dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA), or ospemifene. (Expert Opinion)

key_points.point: Follow-up: reassess response and counsel that treatment may be long term.
key_points.verbatim_quote: Clinicians should counsel patients receiving therapy for GSM that long-term treatment and follow-up may be required to manage signs and symptoms. (Clinical Principle)
key_points.location: Statement 26 (Statement 25: reassess to monitor response), Follow-up

key_points.point: The panel advocated relabeling of the estrogen boxed warning, which links this guideline to the AUGS advisory.
key_points.verbatim_quote: the panel appreciates the impact of current boxed warning of estrogen products and advocates for national efforts to update these labels to reflect contemporary literature, particularly regarding low-dose vaginal estrogen.

findings.cluster: Coding commentaries (AUGS Commentary, Coding; Urogynecology 2025-2026). CLUSTER-LEVEL ACCESS NOTE: all nine are 2-page AUGS commentaries with no PubMed abstract. I checked every one through LWW/Ovid (WebFetch returned HTTP 402; curl and the browser pane showed "Full Text Access for Subscribers ... Log in with your American Urogynecologic Society credentials"). Europe PMC reports them as not open access, and no copy exists in reports/audit-v2/sources-local or ~/Downloads (the Downloads PDF "AUGS Clinical Guidance for Everyday Practice.pdf" only lists the titles). Access for all nine is therefore TITLE-ONLY, plus PubMed metadata and, where present, PubMed reference lists. No recommendation from any of the nine documents is stated below. The user is an AUGS member and can log in with AUGS credentials, save the nine PDFs and extract them into reports/audit-v2/sources-local/ to close these items. To make the proposed edits concrete, I checked the WARWIKI statements against public primary or official sources I did read in full and quote each one: CMS MLN1783722 (April 2026, modifier 59/X{EPSU}), CMS MLN Matters MM13473 (G2211, revised April 2025), the CMS CY2026 PFS final-rule fact sheet (CMS-1832-F), the AUA CY2026 PFS summary, the SGO Coding Corner (+99459), and the Medtronic 2026 sacral and PTNS and 2025 implantable-tibial coding and payment guides, which cite the CMS CY2026 PFS final-rule addenda for wRVUs. Main WARWIKI findings: (1) docs/08-resources/hidden-curriculum/billing-coding.mdx has wrong 2026 wRVUs and a mislabelled programming code in its SNM and PTNS rows (95970 is 'without programming', not 'simple programming'; 95971 is missing). (2) The same page has no T codes, no modifier 25, no E/M, no G2211 and no +99459 content. (3) healthcare-finance.mdx still states the 2024 conversion factor and never explains budget neutrality. No clinical page (SNM, PNE, PTNS, ITNS, urodynamics) carries CPT codes, and none should, per scope. Worth a short, year-stamped addition: the SNM/PTNS table corrections, T-code rows, modifier 25 plus the X{EPSU}-over-59 rule, and a one-paragraph E/M note. Too transient for more than one line each: G2211, +99459, and the budget-neutrality figures (explain the concept, date the numbers). Housekeeping: the task URL for the budget-neutrality commentary (journals.lww.com/fpmrs/fulltext/2026/05000/budget_neutrality,...1.aspx) actually redirects to a different article, the AUGS POP best practice statement (doi 10.1097/SPV.0000000000001641); the correct DOI is 10.1097/SPV.0000000000001827. Also, one attempt to open a Medtronic PDF in the Browser pane triggered a file-save dialog on the user's screen; I did not retry and read the PDFs via WebFetch instead. items.change: Correct the SNM rows to CY2026 values and descriptors, labelled 'CY2026 Medicare PFS': 95970 relabelled 'without programming' at 0.35 (page has 0.45); add the missing 95971 at 0.78; 95972 at 0.80 (page has 1.92); 64561 at 5.30 (page has 8.20); 64590 at 4.97 (page has 5.10) with the revised descriptor; 64585 at 2.06 (page has 5.60); 64595 at 3.70 (page has 3.80); 64581 left for verification.
items.reason: The current text is as quoted: lines 247-253 give 64561 8.20, 64581 10.40, 64585 5.60, 64590 5.10, 64595 3.80, 95970 'simple programming' 0.45 and 95972 1.92. There is no 95971 row anywhere on the page, and the page carries no year label. Two independent CY2026 manufacturer guides agree on every value. (1) Medtronic's SNM 2026 guide (physician table 'Effective January 1, 2026 – December 31, 2026', work RVUs sourced to 'PFS 2026 Final Rule CMS-1832-F Addenda') gives 64561 5.30, 64590 4.97, 64585 2.06, 64595 3.70, 95970 0.35 ('...sacral nerve, neurostimulator pulse generator/ transmitter, without programming'), 95971 0.78 and 95972 0.80. (2) Boston Scientific's 2026 SNM guide (sourced to CMS-1832-F Addendum B) gives the identical values. The 64590 descriptor ('peripheral, sacral, or gastric ... requiring pocket creation and connection between electrode array and pulse generator or receiver') is the version in force since the CPT revision effective 1 January 2024; Boston Scientific's guide still prints the old 'direct to inductive coupling' wording, so use Medtronic's. I could not verify 64581 (10.40) from any public source; neither guide lists it. Nothing here depends on the AUGS commentary, which remains title-only (Ovid paywall; no local copy in sources-local or Downloads). The correction stands on the CMS-sourced guides; cite the AUGS piece only once it has been read.

Medtronic's 2025 implantable tibial neuromodulation guide (physician table 'Effective January 1, 2025 – December 31, 2025') lists 0816T, 0818T, 0589T and 0590T, each with 'N/A' Medicare work RVUs and 'Carrier priced' office and facility payment. items.reason: The Modifiers table (lines 588-610) lists 22, 50, 51, 52, 53, 58, 59, 62, 66, 74, 76-80, 82, AS, XE, XS, XP, XU and LT/RT. It has no modifier 25, and the 59 row reads only 'Different session, site, organ, incision, lesion, or injury — document clearly'. The CMS MLN booklet MLN1783722 (April 2026, read from the PDF) states: 'Note: Modifier 59 should not be appended to an E/M service. To report a separate and distinct E/M service with a non-E/M service performed on the same date, see modifier 25.' It also states: 'These modifiers give greater reporting specificity in situations where you used modifier 59 previously. Use these modifiers instead of modifier 59 whenever possible. Only use modifier 59 if no other more specific modifier is appropriate.' The current 22/51/59 wording does not contradict CMS. This is durable, surgeon-relevant content on the designated billing page. The Molden 2026 commentary is inaccessible, but this edit does not depend on it.
